en: Now, therefore, I shall explain the secret [teaching] characterized by perfect meditative absorption (samyaksamādhi), by which Śrī Heruka is attained with reverence; no other exists. //1//
From the process of dissolution up to the process of evolution, the manifestation of the *nirmāṇakāya* is clearly indicated;
for here, everything beginning with the *dharmakāya* and the *sambhogakāya* is indeed condensed. //2//
Having first reached a solitary place such as a mountain and so forth, one should construct a cemetery there and offer a bali-oblation to the guardians of that field. //3//

The Yogin should cause [the deity] to accept the *argha* and other offerings, preceded by the cleansing of the mouth; having assumed a form, the Blessed One has taught [this practice] as described in the meditations on cloth-paintings (*paṭa*) and so forth. //4//

Possessing the purpose of benefiting the world through meditative cultivation, one should instantly take as an object of focus the extremely terrible seat of the hungry ghosts (pretāsana), which accomplishes everything for everyone. //5//
The syllable Śrī is considered to be for the sake of all beings, both external and internal;
these are of the nature of the conventional (saṃvṛti), while the absolute (vivṛti) is that which leads to the end of suffering. //6//
Having reached every location,
[he offers] the bali-oblation to the guardians of that cremation ground.
The Blessed One, possessing the purity of a yogin, should manifest his form for the sake of all beings, for the purpose of all things, as the essence of the syllable Śrī.
The concealment (*saṃvṛti*) and the revelation (*vivṛti*), as well as other such [states], are described by the syllable *Śrī* through non-duality;
and by the syllable *He*, all those belonging to one's own mandala, such as Heruka and the rest, [are drawn] from the heart. (7)
The earth and other elements arise from the totality of mental cultivation;
they consist of the nature of emptiness as their cause, and there is no conceptualization of them as having the nature of a cause or the like. //8//
The selflessness of phenomena in terms of intrinsic nature is emptiness; the array of the vehicle of yoga is the great web of conceptual construction regarding the selflessness of the person. //9//

And since that which consists of the suffix *ru* has departed from my mental construction (*vyūha*), what need is there to speak further regarding the entirety of non-duality through knowledge as taught by me? (10)
Because it does not abide anywhere and because it is devoid of the letter "ka," it is not empty of the perception of existence, but possesses the beautiful form of the mere thing-in-itself. //11//

O Goddess, the meditation on the state of Śrī Heruka is all-pervading; first, one should visualize the self-arisen seed-syllable of primordial wisdom in the center of a sun and lotus within the heart. (12)
The syllable *he* arises as Heruka and so forth through meditative cultivation;
it is emptiness, not having the nature of causes and so forth.
That practitioner of yoga perceives the empty array of the net of persons as being the letter *ru*, yet that array is devoid of self;
what more need be said of those established in non-duality who perceive the letter *ka*?

—Surūpaka— Heruka, O Goddess, all-pervading, all-pervading (271). In the centers, [the seed-syllables] ABCD; in the centers, the seed-syllables ABC (D). 74. One should emit rays of light of various colors, filling the sky.
Having drawn forth the deity as a net in the form of the Jñānaḍākinīs (13/273).
One should establish the Lord of the World situated in the center of the hollow of space;

having performed worship with nectar and other offerings, and having confessed one's sins and so forth, one should recollect her whose nature is born from the moon and sun, and who is characterized by compassion and the rest.

One should visualize the pure yoga as having emptiness as its essential nature. (15) One should point out that the peaked pavilion has the five seed-syllables as its essential nature. (276) Subsequently, one should clearly [visualize] the Causal Vajradhara upon a lotus atop Mount Meru. (16) (278)
White in color, with four faces, three eyes, and twelve arms; his nature is the union with Prajñā, and he is adorned with the ornaments of a youth. //279-177//
White, green, and red, with yellow swirls on the left;
he has a face, matted hair, and a crown, and holds a double-vajra and a half-moon;
he stands in the *ālīḍha* posture, treading upon Hara and Gaurī. //280–282//
A vajra and a bell, an elephant hide, a ḍamaru drum, and a flaying knife; likewise, an axe, a trident, a khaṭvāṅga staff, an alms bowl, and a noose. //19//283–284//

272 And rays of light fill the sky; 273 [one should visualize] the deity in form; 274 one should establish the Lord situated in the midst of the firmament; 275 by means of [the syllables] *Tā* and so forth, [he is] arisen from the sun; 276 [he is] pure by virtue of his own essential nature; 277 the palace is of the nature of that [same] essence; 278–281 [it is] white in color like Mount Meru, with an eye, with arms, white and yellow in the swirls, with faces, matted hair, and the universe; 282 established as Hara and Gaurī; 283 [holding] an elephant-goad, a hand-drum, and a flaying-knife; 284 an axe, a trident, and a noose; 58 59 61 62 a severed head on the left and right, upon the forty-eight petals. //20//
Upon the lotus of universal colors, there is a twelve-spoked wheel;
within the delightful cremation ground consisting of thirty-two doors and sixteen gateways,
there is a curved knife, a jewel-vajra, a lotus-wheel, and a sword.
The universal vajra, the skull-cup, the severed head, the skeleton, and the lord;
22/289 the noose or the goad should be known [as such] in the row of wheels within the wheel.
290 Each [wheel] has thirty-six spokes, and the vajra-lotus is like the sun. 23/291
The transformed causal vajra, numbering fifty-four and so forth, is always the perfected mandala-circle through the sounds of the songs. //292, 24//
The Lord, who is the invitation to the world and the source of splendor, says: "Who are you? Listen, O gatekeeper!
Arise, O Lord whose nature is compassion; grant me the vessel for the bliss of desire. [293] 294.
On the left and right, on the lotuses of forty-eight petals, the universe—
287. The sixteen cremation grounds;
288. The wheel of the flaying knife and the sword; 289. The skull and the lord.
One should know the noose or the goad; the lotus with thirty spokes, the sun, and the vajra with fifty, four, and so forth. *jagaï nimanta* (ABCD; cf.
*nimanta* R and *manta* V); *nudihi* (ABCD; cf.
*nudihi* R and *nuvihī* V); *pāhu* (AB); *pahū* (CD).
O Lord (pahu), you (tumi) have heard (suṇa).
*Note: Variants include *ke* for *R* and *V*; *tumī* for *R* and *V*; and *sūṇa* for *D*.*

Having heard [the words], the Lord entered; having heard [them], the Lord rose up. "Who are you, O Lord? I am one who has entered. "Rise up, O Lord! "I have indeed risen. Notes: * *surṇṇa* (R), *śuna* (V), and *sunna* (ABC) correspond to the past participle of the root *śru* ("to hear").

* *paveśagao* (D); cf. *praveśagate* (R) and *pavesao* (V). * The Lord (*pahu*) asks: "Who are you? and the other replies: "I am one who has entered" (*suṇa paveśagao*). * The Lord says: "Rise up" (*utha pahu em*); the response is:

"I have indeed risen" (*utha hu*, *uṭham hu*, *uṭhaka*). * Variants: *utha* (AC), *uṭham* (B), *uṭhaka* (D). The form *uṭha* corresponds to the imperative of the root *utthā* ("to rise"). Note that *hu* is used as an emphatic particle meaning "indeed" or "certainly. * Cf. the variants provided for comparison.
*utha* R and V; *karuṇa* AB; *varuṇa* C; *ruṇa* D; cf.
*karuṇa* R and *ruṇā* V; *sabhāvu* em.; *satāthu* ABCD; cf.
[He] is honored by the virtuous (satātha) and esteemed (matāthu); [he] desires greatness (mahu), and [he] desires great happiness (mahasuha).
Great bliss (mahāsuha) R and great bliss (mahasuha) V; vājjadharu ABD; vajjadharu C; cf.
vājjudharu R and vājjadhanna V. 76. Listen, listen! Just as a beast in the slaughterhouse goes toward its death, so too does this world, though it enjoys pleasure, go toward its destruction. //26//

O Mother, O Ramā, O wielder of the thunderbolt, your innate nature cannot be described by words. (296) The cause of the seven worlds, you are the essence of all righteousness; why do you remain in this innate nature that cannot be sung? (297) Like a staff, you are empty and devoid of purpose. (27) (299)
Arise! You whose nature is compassion, who desire my great bliss, wielder of the thunderbolt—listen, listen! (A; *suṇḍa* B, C, D; cf.
*suṇu suṇu* R and *sumu śu* V) ◊ *para-* ABCD; cf. [variant].
para R and paḥ ra V ◊ -üāru ABCD; cf. uāru R and V ◊ gao ABCD; Tib; cf. gade R and gao V ◊ jima ABCD; cf.
Just as a beast in the world of men, or a demon in the world of the gods, dies—listen, listen!
Even as a beast in the world of men dies, he perishes with his pride shattered. ABCD; cf. *paśuroa* (R) and *ttaroa* (V);
*marantao* (AD) and *marantoo* (BC); cf. *marantade* (R) and *marattoo* (V).
*viasia pamu R* and *viasia pammu V*; *kāma ABCD*; cf.
*kāma R* and *V* ◊ *mahu AB*; *majū C*; *maku D*; cf.
*mahu R* and *maḍā V* ◊ *tima ABCD*; cf. [...]
Just as the world is born from the union [of the elements], so too is the world well-governed by the one who is self-controlled.
Just as the spring season is the delight of passion, so too is the world well-governed by the one who is self-controlled.

Delight! Delight! *Note on the variants:* The reading *loa sabbha* (R) and *llāa saha* (V) correspond to the Sanskrit *lokasambhava*. The variants *suhantao* (AB) and *sudantao* (CD) correspond to the Sanskrit *sudāntataḥ* (well-restrained). The phrase *viasia pammu kāma* (ABD) and *viasia pamu kāma* (C) corresponds to the Sanskrit *vikāsita-pramada-kāmam* (the blossoming of passion and joy). The final *rama rama* (ABD) and *rama ra* (C) is an exclamation of delight. The reconstruction *mahu tima loa sambha sudantao* aligns with the thematic structure of the verse.
O Rama, O Rama! [The reading] *mãi* in R and *ma / i* in V; cf. *māi* in R and *ma / i* in V. ◊ *vajjaharāi* in A, B, D; *vajja aï harāi* in C; cf.
*vajjaharāi* in R and V. *sahaja* (A, B, C, D: born); cf. [the commentary].

Innate (sahaja) and of the same nature (sarūa), it cannot be expressed by speech (na vācāi); it is the mother of delight (rama rama māi), the destroyer of obstacles (vajjahara), innate by nature (sahajasarūa), and beyond the seven worlds (sattaloa para).
The seven worlds beyond, O R and V; the staff has come, O A B; the staff has come, O C; the staff has come, O D; cf.
the tooth has come, O R and the ten have come, O V; just as, O A B C D; cf. just as, O R and V; by you, O A B C D; by you, O R and by you, O V; empty, O A B D; *sumna*, O C; cf. the empty.

Listen, R, and listen, V! Just as the seven worlds are subject to the power of another, so too, O empty one, are you brought to ruin (nikajjaaï). 299. The cause (kāranu) of this is the law of the assembly (sabbha dhammaha). (Note: *nikajjaaï* corresponds to *nikarjjaaï* in R and *kajjaaï* in V;
*kāranu* corresponds to *kāraṇu* in R and *kāranu* in V; *sabbha dhammaha* corresponds to *sabhā dharmmahe* in C.)
I am one who has attained the Dharma together with you all. (R: *sambha dhammaha*; V: *saha dhammaham*) You [plural]...
(A, B, C: *tummi*; D: *tumii*; cf. *tumii* in R and V, and *tummi*). ...you [plural]... (A, B, D: *ke*; C:
*ka*; cf. *ke* in R and V). ...I go [or remain]... (A, B, D: *acchasi*; C: *acchami*; cf. [the respective readings in R and V]).
You desire, R and V; *sahaja*, A B C D; cf.
*sahaja*, R and D; *sarūa*, A D; *sarua*, B C; cf.
*sarūa*, R and *sarua*, V; *na*, A B D; *ra*, C; cf. [variant].
O Kāraṇu, abandon desire through the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), so that you may go to a world equal to me. //28//
300. This [mantra], awakened in accordance with the *Gītā*, is Heruka himself. 301. Oṃ āḥ kāyavākcittavajra hūṃ phaṭ hoḥ. //29//
302–303. One who possesses the yoga of the instantaneous form should recite this mantra; instantly becoming the self that is the mantra, he is the hero of all and [unites with] the Yoginī. 30.
304–305. Bhairava and Kālarātri are upon the sun and fire atop the pericarp; their bodies are in the *tāṇḍava* dance posture, and they are half-black and half-green. 31.
He has seventy-six arms and faces, and possesses three eyes on each of his seventeen heads; the hero wears a crown of matted hair and bears a universal vajra and a half-moon. //32//
His faces on the right and left are always terrifying with great fangs; the remaining faces follow the sequence of yellow and red, while the others are like the color of a bhrṅga bee.
O Lord of the Assembly, why do you remain silent? You do not know your own innate nature;
[the dance] is performed with half-bodies, half-faces, and [half-]arms. [The universe—]

The remaining faces, according to the sequence of yellow and red on the left and right, are known as the *Samputodbhava*. One should understand that the great, fierce, and loud laughter, along with the terrifyingly formidable fangs and the array of weapons, are situated on the left and right in their proper order.
An elephant hide on the two hands, and likewise the *yonimudrā* from the other; and on the right, a vajra, sword, spear, and trident, in due order.
The axe, the scythe, the arrow, the mallet split by the trident, the discus, the hand-drum, the dagger, the staff, and the javelin;
The conch-shell, the trumpet, the staff, the peacock-feather whisk, as well as the crow’s wing, the small key, and the fire-vessel [are located] on the mountain.
The club is the mirror, the lute is the ankle and the hand; the entrails are the Rāhu-noose, the fetter is the prison, and the net is the evil womb.
And the oil-flame of the *kabandha*, and the form of Bhairava in succession;

[the face of the fierce and terrifying *dṛṣṭākarāla-raudra*, the terrifying ones surrounded by Bhairavas, and the great, fierce, boisterous laughter]. [This may be an interpolation, as it is included only in manuscript D (the newest manuscript) and is not translated into Tibetan.]

[The goddess is] terrifying with fangs that are formidable; she is to be known [as holding weapons] on the left and right sides. *Vastram* means a multitude. This line is omitted in C. *Carma* refers to two hands. *Kunta*, *bāṇa*, *bhinnam*, *mudgara*, *daṇḍa*, and *bhiṇḍipālaka* (respectively); PH reads *bhiṇḍimāla* and *bhiṇḍivāla* for *bhindipāla*. *Śaṅkha*, *kāhala*, *mayūra-picchikā* (CD); *pakṣa-m-kūcikā*, *kākapakṣā*, and *kūcikā* (respectively); Ṭākārṇava reads *kākapakṣeṣu kūcikā*.
—[the hand] holding an entrail, [the head of] Rāhu, [and] a shackle; a prison cell (haḍim for haḍir), a noose, and a net, respectively.
—[He holds] flaming oil; in the left [hand], Bhairava holds a bell, a shield, a tusk, a pestle, a noose, and a skull-cup.
A bow, a skull-topped staff, a book, flour-cakes, and a threatening gesture; a garland of rattling bells, a chain, a stone, and the ashes of a cremation ground.
The tongue is the wet hide of a goat; the hanging hair is the *kacadorikā*; the ribs are the fuel-wood for the fire; the anus is the *pharī*; and the head is the skull.
Kaṅkālarātrikā, Netrabukka, Guṇavartikā, Śanaiścara, Kīlaka, and Bījapūrakapattra.
The needle, the body, the skin, the cloud, the rain, the tree, and the blade of grass—thus, in this sequence, the seventy-two weapons are to be understood.
Adorned with ornaments made from five skulls, decorated with the six seals (mudrās), and possessing a garland of a hundred skulls, he has the sound of armlets and anklets.

A pestle of excrement, a skull-cup, flour, the *ghurghura* sound, the cemetery, the *bhokan*, the *ḍakā*, moist hide, a loincloth, a goad, funeral-pyre wood, the anus, the *pharī*, the head, the skeleton, the night, the eye, the palate, Saturn, a ritual stake, the *bījapūraka* fruit, its leaf, needles, body-skin, clouds, trees, a hook, and the weapon of the hand—these are to be known. He is adorned with a garland of five severed heads, a corpse, and ornaments; bracelets jingling with the sound of armlets, he wears a tiger-skin garment, and there is a line of hair upon his body. (333)
In front of him is the Great Goddess Vajravārāhī as described previously;
she holds a vajra-knife in her right hand and a skull-cup in her left,
and embracing the Lord’s waist with both legs, she expresses her passion for him.
She has one face, her hair is disheveled, she is naked, red in color, and wears a garland of severed heads. She is adorned with ornaments of erotic sentiment and a necklace of skulls.
Her limbs are anointed with divine perfumes, and she is endowed with anklets and armlets. She is decorated with divine flower-garlands and embellished with the six mudrās.
She has three eyes, wears a garland of heads, and is adorned with jewel ornaments; she blazes like the fire of universal destruction, radiant with great majesty.

Moist with the bliss of wisdom and means due to their embrace at all the joints; wearing a tiger-skin garment, with a line of hair on her body; O Vārāhī, as before—embracing the Blessed One’s waist with her sword-blade, adorned with the colors of the erotic sentiment, with ornaments, a head-ornament, armlets, and a garland of flowers; thus adorned, one should visualize her as radiant with splendor and light, shimmering with the various flames of Heruka. //50//

The practitioner should cause a silk garland to be placed upon the heads of them all; on the lotus petals, starting from the east and so forth, the Yoginīs should be positioned in their respective intermediate spaces. //51//
The twenty-four [deities] beginning with Ḍākinī are enumerated as six groups of six; likewise, from the east to the north, there are six [groups] beginning with Ḍākinī. //52//

The six beginning with Uttarā extend to the end of the West; then again, the group of six beginning with Lāmā extends from the West to the South; and the family beginning with Khaṇḍarohā [extends] likewise. //53//
Then there are the six beginning with Dakṣiṇā and ending with Pūrvāntā, and those beginning with Rūpiṇī; namely, Ḍākinī, Rūpikā, Cumbikā, and Parāvṛtā. //54//
Sabālikā, Anuvartinī, Kṛṣṇārdhakā, Haritārdhakā, Lāmā, Yogeśvarī, Bhadrā, Kapālinī, and Kaṅkālikā. //55//
Rājāvartī has half green and half red [parts] extending in sequence; Khaṇḍarohā, Śmaśānī, Vidrāvī, and Kurukullikā [are likewise]. //56//
The weeping one, the actress, the narrator, the red one, the half-yellow one, the yellowish one, Rūpiṇī, Bhairavī, Śekhi, Śikhaṇḍin, Jaṭilī, and Rudrā. //57//
The goddess Vārāhikā is half yellow and half black, possessing arms, weapons, and so forth; and within the petals are skull-cups containing the five nectars. //58//
Standing in the pratyālīḍha posture and bearing a garland of skull-bowls and other ornaments, she is to be known as born from the upper part of Mount Sumeru, revolving counter-clockwise. (59)
Thus is the lotus petal (60). Outside of that is the vajra-circle, and in the center of the blue-black [mandala] are Ḍākinī, Lāmā, Khaṇḍarohā, and Rūpiṇī (61).

The goddesses Kṛṣṇārdhā, Bhujā, Astrā, and the others are like five skull-cups of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) upon the petals; they are situated in the counter-clockwise direction starting from the left [petal] above the summit of Mount Sumeru. Thus, on the lotus petals outside of that, in the center of Kṛṣṇa, are Ḍākinī, Lāmā, Khaṇḍarohā, Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍākṣī, Prabhāvatī, Mahānāsā, Vīramatī, Kharvarī, Laṅkeśvarī, Drumacchāyā, Airāvatī, and likewise Mahābhairavī; Vāyuvegā, Surābhakṣī, Śyāmādevī, Subhadrikā, Hayakarṇā, Khagānanā, Cakravegā, Khaṇḍarohikā, Śauṇḍinī, Cakravarmiṇī, Suvīrā, Mahābalā, Cakravartinī, Mahāvīryā, Yāminī, Yuminī, Sañcālinī, Trāsanī, Caṇḍikā, Sarasvatī, Icchāsiddhi, and Mahājvālā. Their colors correspond to those in the wheels (*cakra*). They have four arms, one face, and hold a skull-cup (*kapāla*) and a *khaṭvāṅga*; likewise, they hold a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*) and a flaying-knife (*kartti*), with loose hair, naked, their bodies adorned with the five mudrās and garlands of vajras, seated upon corpses (*pretāsana*), most terrible yoginīs in all the wheels. They are endowed with various ornaments and likewise possessed of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*). Thus, the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is declared to be the sacred seat (*pīṭha*). The stage known as Pramuditā is the secondary seat (*upapīṭha*) and so forth. Among the single stages, twelve stages are intended. In this way, it should be understood that all [deities] in all the elements (*dhātu*) are of one nature. The All-pervading Lord (*vibhu*) is said to consist of thirty-six [deities]. And thus is the essential nature of the heroes (*vīra*) and yoginīs of the elements. [The sequence is: Sañcālinī, Trāsanī, Caṇḍikā, Sarasvatī, Icchāsiddhi, Mahājvālā, and Varṇā in the wheels. In the wheels, they have one face, loose hair, are naked, their bodies are adorned [with mudrās], they are seated upon corpses in the wheels, endowed with ornaments, and possessed of wisdom and means. The formless realm is declared to be the sacred seat. The stages, the seats (*pīṭha*), and the secondary seats (*upapīṭha*)—among the single stages, there are twelve. In this way, it should be understood that among the single elements, the All-pervading Lord is said to consist of thirty-six. This is the essential nature of the yoginīs of the elements. Having brought forth the beings in the circular rims (*cakravāḍa*) according to the sequence of families (386).
Furthermore, those thirty-six are divided according to their respective locations in sequence.
(71) Thus ends the first, the Vajracakra. (72) Now, I shall further describe this Heart-Cakra outside of that. (389)
In the red and yellow-colored [sections], and likewise in the middle of the spokes of the wheel:
Vajradharī, Akṣobhyī, Vairocanī, Ratneśikā, Padmanartī, Amoghī, Locanā, and Māmakī. //73–74//390–392//
Pāṇḍarā, Tārā, Rūpavajrā, as well as Śabda, Gandha, and Rasa; Sparśavajrā, Dharmadhātuvajrā, Kṣitigarbha, and Khagarbha. 393–394.

Having generated the family [of deities] in the thirty-six directions, first—on the outer wheel—among these syllables, in the center are: Vajradharī, Akṣobhyī, Vairocanī, Ratneśikā, Padmanartī, Amoghalocanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍarā, Tārā, Rūpavajrā, Śabdavajrā, Gandhavajrā, Rasavajrā, Sparśavajrā, Dharmadhātuvajrā, Kṣitigarbhī, Khagarbhakī, Pāṇī, Lokanāthī, and Lokanāthī. Sarvaṇī (C, D); cf. Samantabhadrī, Samantaprabhā (A, B, C); Samantraprabhī (D). Note that this is not the name of a bodhisattva.
Ratnolkā, Nairātmyā, Bhṛkuṭī, and Paṇṇasorikā. //76//
Yamāntakī, Prajñāntikī, Padmāntikī, and Vighnāntikī; Acalā, Nīladaṇḍī, Takkirājī, and Mahābalā;
Uṣṇīṣā and Sumbharājñī—whatever their colors are in the [various] wheels, the remaining characteristics, such as their faces and so forth, are the same as those in the Vajracakra.

One should contemplate the goddesses in the secondary seats (*upapīṭha*) with their respective male consorts (*upāya*). This should also be understood to apply to all the wheels (*cakra*) by means of the *pratyālīḍha* stance.
The realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and Vimalā are considered the first continent.
[The goddesses are] Yamāntakī (or Yamāntikī), Prajñāntakī (or Prajñāntikī), Padmāntakī (or Padmāntikī), and Vighnāntakī (or Vighnāntikā). (79)

Acalī (A Bpc C; acalā D; acarī); cf. J, acaliye and acalī R, and acalā V. Nīladaṇḍī (A Bpc C; nīradaḍī D); cf. ba J, ṭakkirājīye and nīradaṇḍī R, and nīladaṇḍā V. Ṭakkirājī (A; ṭakkirājā Bpc; ṭarkirāja C; ṭakkīrājī D); cf. J, nīladaṇḍīya and ṭakkirājī R, and ṭakkirāja V. Mahābalā (A Bpc C; mahābalī D); cf. mahābaliye and mahābamahābali R, and mahābalā V.

*Uṣṇīṣā* (ABpc; *uṣṇīṣa* C; *uṣṇīṣī* D; cf. *vajroṣṇīsīye* J, *ūṣṇīṣacakrīye* and *uṣṇīṣā* R, and *uṣṇīṣā* V); *sumbharājñī ca* (ABpcC; *sumbharājīm ca* D; cf. J, *sumbharājīye* and *sumbharājī* R, and *sumbharājī* V); *varṇa* (ABpcCD; cf. *varṇa* V and *b*, and *b* of the *Dākārṇava*);
*cakre tu* (ABpcCD; cf. *yādṛśām* AC, *yāśām* Bpc, *yādṛśam* D; cf. *yādṛśam* *Ṭākārṇava* and *yādṛśām* V).
In the wheels [of the body], one should recognize the characteristic; he should know the leader, who is desired as Laghuheruka. //80//

Padmaheruka is held to be in the third, and Ākāśaka in the fourth; Bhairambha in the fifth, and Heru in the sixth is held to be Addhitheruka. Jvālaheru is in the seventh, and Dravaheruka in the eighth; Jñānaheru is in the ninth, and Cittaheruka in the tenth. Vāk-heruka is in the eleventh, and Kāyika is held to be in the twelfth. These twelve are Mahāvajraheruka, and not from any other tantra.
A wise man should observe the configuration of Heruka as the Three-Circle Saṃvara within them, as well as their respective colors in each of the wheels (cakras).
Thus ends the second [wheel], the heart wheel.
Now, outside of that is the wheel named Sarvaguṇa, which is white and red; one should place the thirty-six excellent ḍākinīs starting from the center of the vajra spokes.

The Brāhmaṇī, Kṣatriṇī, Vaiśyī, Śūdrī, Caṇḍālinī, and Sucī—[these are] Heruka (ABD; Herukai C). In the third [case] (A; tṛtīyam BC; tṛtīya D), [and] in the fourth (AC; caturthyām BD; cf. caturthyām V), the Kāśaka view (AB; kāśakam C; kāśakarmmatam D) is held.

Bhairambha (Bhairambham A; Bhairambha BD; Bhairava C). Heruḥ (ABCD; cf. *heruḥ* V and *-herum* Ṇākārṇava). *Ddhi*terukam (A; *dvi*herukam B; *ṛddhi*heruka C; *dvi*herukam D; cf. *dviheluka* R, though it is unmetrical). *Matam* (ABCD). *Jvāla*- (ABC; *jvāra* D). *-heruñ* (ABD; *herukam* C). *-heruñ* (ABD; *herukam* C).
—*heruñ* A*B heru C; *ppharukam* D. *kāyikam* ABC *kāpikam* D. *dvādaśa* ABD *dvādaśam* C. *nānyatantrataḥ* ABD *nānyataḥ* C.
*saṃsthānam* ACD *sasthānam* B (ApcBCD *heru* Aac).
The letter *varṇa* is ABC, and the second is *varṇṇa* D; the second is C, and [the first] is ABD.

Among them, the wise man possesses the restraint (*saṃvara*) of ABCD; their names are Rāmā C, [and] Trimśā ABD (or trimśad D). [They are] Dhūtikā ABD (or dhūtīkā); Sūcī, Ḍombī, Naṭī, Kapālinī, Kaivartī, and Veṇunaṭī //87//
Śaṅkhinī, Tantuvāpī, Kandunī, Kāṣṭhakārikā, Mālinī, Tailinī, Chekā, Kośakārī, and Dhūtinī. //88//

The *haḍagāḍī*, the courtesan (*gaṇikā*), the *kallavālī*, the *kūparī*, the female royal soldier (*rājabhaṭī*), the butcher’s wife (*khaṭṭikī*), and the betel-seller (*tāmbūlavikrayī*)—these indeed [are the types]. //89//

The goldsmith, the blacksmith, the jeweler, the weaver, the *ḍombī*, the actress, the skull-bearer, the fisherwoman, the flute-player, the conch-blower, the weaver of cloth, the potter, the woodcutter, the garland-maker, the oil-presser, the *cchepī*, the silkworm-rearer, the procuress, the *haḍagāḍī*, the courtesan, the water-carrier, the *kūparī*, the royal soldier, the butcher, and the betel-seller—likewise the goldsmith, the blacksmith, the jeweler, the weaver, the barbarian woman, the *oḍinī*, the merchant woman, the stone-cutter, and the female cultivator. //90//
And the leather-worker is a yoginī; in those respective wheels of colors, everything else is to be understood just as it is in the heart wheel. 422/91.
One should understand that the field here consists of all the families of the desire realm; they call one's own [field] the second island, which consists of wisdom and means. //92//
And the Prabhākarī stage itself is to be worshipped as the Guru personally; it is proclaimed that [the mantras] begin with the Praṇava and consist of the recitation of one's own name. //42, 93//
One should perform [the ritual] in all the wheels (cakras) ending with *hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*. Outside of that, one should provide a circle consisting of two lines, black and blue.
The gateway, archway, and altar are adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces; at the eastern doors and in the center is Kākāsyā, from whom the Ḍākinīs arise.

The goldsmith, the blacksmith, the jeweler, the weaver, the barbarian woman, the Oḍinī, the merchant, the stonemason, the farmer, and the leather-worker— among these castes and crafts, the remainder should be understood; here, the field of the heart is said to be the second, consisting of all families,
and one's own ground is itself to be worshipped.

The worship is proclaimed as being performed with mantras consisting of the utterance of their own names. One should cause them to be placed at the ends of the syllables *kā*. On the exterior, one should provide a circular [enclosure] adorned with lines, gates, altars (*vedi*), necklaces (*hāra*), and beautiful ornaments.

At the gate and in the center is Kākāsyā; since Ḍākinī is there, Ulūkāsyā is in the north, while Śvānavaktrikā is in the west. Sūkarāsyā is in the south, and the supreme Lāmā and the others are in their respective colors. Yamadāḍhī, Dūtī, Daṃṣṭrī, and Mathanī reside in the corners of Agni, Nairṛtya, Vāyu, and Īśāna respectively. Two by two, they should be made equal in color according to their faces, in due order.

In the east, north, west, and south, one should always fashion the grounds as black, blue, yellow, red, and yellow in color; thus is the Sahaja-maṇḍala, because it consists of four wheels. Subsequently, the wheels of the Nirmāṇa, Saṃbhoga, and Dharma [bodies] should be made in their proper order: the second wheel has three lines, the third has four lines, and the fourth consists of five lines; the cremation ground is to be placed in sequence all around.

In the south is Sūkarāsyā; her color is blue (lāma), and she is supreme. In the southeast, northwest, northeast, and southwest corners are Yamadāḍhī, Dūtī, Daṃṣṭrī, and Mathanī, respectively, according to their forms. They are blue, green, red, and yellow in color. The innate mandala consists of four circles and four wheels. Following that, the emanation [mandala] should be constructed in sequence as the second wheel: having three lines, four lines, and consisting of five lines. One should fashion the cremation ground on all sides, circular in shape, and considered to have outer grounds and so forth. The wheel consisting of five lines is square and brilliantly radiant.

Therein, the cremation grounds (*śmaśāna*) of the innate wheel (*sahajacakra*) are described: Candogragahvara, Jvālākulakaraṅkaka, and Vibhīṣaṇa are situated to the left in the directions starting from the east; Aṭṭaṭṭahāsa is in the northeast, Lakṣmīvana in the southeast, Ghorāndhakāra in the southwest, and Kilikilārava in the northwest. These cremation grounds are of terrifying form, filled with the cries of *vetāḍas*, spirits, and jackals.
In this sequence, one should dwell in the eight cremation grounds: the tree, the guardian of the direction, the lord of nāgas, and the lord of clouds, respectively;
likewise, the śirīṣa, aśvattha, kaṅkeli, mango, and vaṭa trees, as well as the karañja, the creeper, the parkaṭi, and the pārthiva.

One should make it circular in shape; the outer part is considered to have five lines at its corners. The cremation grounds (*śmaśāna*) are described as follows: Caṇḍogra-gahvara, Gahvara-jvālākula-karaṅka, Vibhīṣaṇa situated to the left with a loud *aṭṭaṭṭahāsa* laugh, Lakṣmīvana in the northeast (*īśāna*), Ghorāndhakāra in the southeast (*hutāśana*), and Kilikilārava in the northwest (*vāyavya*). These are the forms of the cremation grounds, which should be positioned in this sequence along with the sounds of jackals (*śivā*). Furthermore, in order, there are the trees, the guardians of the directions (*dikpāla*), the *nāgas*, and the lords of the clouds: Śirīṣa, Aśvattha, Kaṅkeli, Cūta, Karañja, and the Latāparkaṭi tree. Then Indra, Dhanada (Kubera), the Lord of Nāgas, and Yamādhipa; Īśāna, Hutāśana, Rākṣasendra, and Anilādhipa; Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Karkoṭa, Padma, Mahāpadma, Huluhulu, Kulika, Śaṅkhapālaka, Garjita, Ghūrṇita, Ghora, Āvarta, Ghana, Pūraṇa, Varṣaṇa, and Caṇḍa—these are the lords of the clouds. One should cause the circle of vajras (*vajrāvalī*) to be drawn here in all the cremation grounds. Everything here, both external and internal, should be performed in this very way. This is the third wheel of qualities (*guṇacakra*), the first enclosure (*puṭa*). Now, the outer wheel of space (*ākāśacakra*) resembles a blue lotus. In the center of the thirty-six spokes is this Yoginī Khecarī. [The goddesses are: Kinnarī, Gandhārī, Huntakī, and Pāṭavī. [The directional deities are: Dhanada, Nāgendra, Yamādhipa, Īśāna, Hutāśana, Anilādhipa, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Karkoṭa, Padma, Mahāpadma, Huluhulu, Kulika, Śaṅkha, Ghūrṇita, Āvarta, Ghana, Pūraṇa, Varṣaṇa, and the lords of the clouds. Here in all the cremation grounds, the circle of vajras must be made; this is the third wheel, the first enclosure, the space in the center. [The musical instruments and their presiding goddesses are: Khecarī, Kinnarī, Gandhārī, Vīṇā, Vaṃśā, Mukundā, Murujā, Gaggarikā, Kāṃsā, Selendrikī, Gītā, Karaḍā, Tamaḍā, Nṛtyā, Lāsyā, Ḍukkā, Tālī, Sāraṇā, Dundubhikā, Modrī, Tānī, Pañcamā, Nālavī, and Ṭambhakī.

The *ḍamarī*, the *duṇḍukī*, the *kāhalī*, and likewise the *orakī*; the *bhūki*, the bell (*ghaṇṭā*), the small bell (*kiṅkiṇī*), and likewise the *ghughurī* and the *ḍukolikā*; the *kāṃsā*, the *selendrikī*, the *gītā*, the *karaḍā*, and the *tamaḍā*.

Nṛtyā, Lāsyā, Ḍukkā, Tālī, Sāraṇā, Dundubhikā, Modrī, Tānī, Pañcamā, Nālavī, Ṭambhakī, Ḍamarī, Dundukī, Kāhalī, Orakī, Pāṭavī, Vīṇā, Vaṃśā, Mukundā, Mukuṃdā, Murujā, Gaggarikā, Kāṃsā, Selendrikī, Gītā, Karaḍā, Tamaḍā, Nṛtyā, Lāsyā, Ḍukkā, Tālī, Sāraṇā, Dundubhikā, Modrī, Tānī, Pañcamā, Nālavī, Ṭambhakī, Ḍamarī, Dundukī, Kāhalī, Orakī, Bhūkī, Ghaṇṭā, Kiṅkiṇī, Ghughurī, Ḍukolikā, Śāṅkhī, Ghoṣavatī, Parṣadā, and Parameśvarī. //117//
The color is various and multicolored, or else it has the appearance of a wheel; it dwells in a secondary field (upakṣetra), and the other [type] belongs to the third continent. //118//
The Khecarī-kula comes and remains here in this island; that is indeed the Arciṣmatī stage, the mistress of her own respective seats and fields. //119//
Sometimes, setting aside the hand-drum (ḍamaru) and the skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), one may also perform the symbolic gestures (abhinaya) of their respective emblems here as desired. //120//
One should cause the lord of the [respective] family to be placed upon the crowns of all the cakras; for here, they consist of wisdom and means according to their noble lineage. //121//
The remaining [details], such as the many ornaments and so forth, should be performed as before. She has three eyes, and in all the cakras she is followed by those who wear no clothes. 122.
Thus ends the first [chapter] of the Ākāśacakra. 123.

Outside of that is the wind-wheel (*vāyucakra*), which is blackish-blue in color. The goddess Śāṅkhī, accompanied by her retinue, the Ghoṣavatī assembly, is the Supreme Sovereign (*parameśvarī*). Her color is that of the *upakṣetra*; she dwells in the third island and is a sky-farer (*khecarī*) here on this ground. She belongs to the Arciṣmatī stage, is the mistress of the sacred seat (*pīṭha*), and possesses the skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*). Here too, one should cause the gestures (*abhinaya*) of the symbols to be performed according to one's preference. She is the sovereign of the wheels upon her crown, consisting of the noble self; she should have many ornaments and eyes. In all the wheels, she wears the directions as her garment (*digambaradharā*). [The reading *digambaradharāḥ* is found in B; *pañcamudrādigambarāḥ* in C; BC omit the rest. Thus it is said. Outside of that, from the center of the vajra, the yoginīs should be placed in their proper order. (124)
The wise one should know that Ākāśagarbha has another name; [the female deities] are Garuḍī, Haṃsī, Citrī, Kākī, Bakī, and Tittirikā. //125//
The peahen, the copper-crested cock, the gudabulikā, the komalā, the female pigeon, the large crow, the gaḍinī, and the kapiñjalī. //126//
Sukī, Mantrī, Sārasā, Gṛddhrā, Ulūkī, Caṭikā, Kāṣṭhacaṭī, Cakravākī, Vṛkṣāraṇī, and Karkavī. //127//

Jalakākī, Katbilāḍī, Nīlagrīvī, Sārikā, Bharanīlakā, Garuḍī, Haṃsī, Citrī, Kākī, Bakī, Tittirikā, Mayūrī, Tāmracūḍī, Gudabulikā, Komalā, Pārāvatī, Bṛhatkākī, Gaḍinī, Kapiñjalī, Sukī, Mantrī, Sārasā, Gṛddhā, Ulūkī, Caṭikā, Kāṣṭhacaṭī, Cakravākī, Vṛkṣāraṇī, Karkavī, Jalakākī, Katbilāḍī, and Nīlagrīvī—these are known as the [deities]. *Senā, Kuṅkumalolā, Vāṭirī, and Kākajaṅghakī.* (128)
Sāmā, Lehapiṣṭā, Daddarī, and Sṛgālinī—such is the circle of Yoginīs, and the color of the earth-circle is as follows. 129.
Alternatively, the arms and so forth are to be known from their respective [mantras] as before; all are of the nature of wisdom and means, and the supreme one dwells in the *cchandoha*. 130.
The stage known as Sudurjayā (Hard to Conquer) is considered to consist of four continents; these three wheels, born from eggs, are distinguished by their qualities. //131//
The third wheel, consisting of three aspects, is that which has the nature of moisture-born beings;
the fourth wheel, named "womb-born," is likewise considered to consist of three aspects. //132//
Thus ends the second wheel, that of Vāyu.
Now, I shall describe from the outside the wheel following this, known by the name Medinī.
(cf. *vajranālagrīvāyai* J, *nīragrīvāye* and *nīragrīvi* R, and *nālagrīvi* V; see also *nīlākṣa* and *nīlākṣī*).
Alternatively, her name may be edited as *nālagrīvī*, in accordance with Tib, J, and V.

[sārikā] AD; mārikā BC; cf. *vajrasārikīye* J, *sārikāye* and *sārikī* R, *mālikā* V, and *śārikā* and *sārikā* (senā) ABCD; cf. *vajrasenāyai* J, *senīye* and *senā* R, and *senā* V; see also *sena* PH. *kunkumalolā* [corr.]

*kumkumarolā* (A); *kumkumalā* (B); *ṅkukumamūlā* (C); *kumkumalo* (D); cf. *vajrakumkumalolāye* (J), *kumkumarolāya* and *kunkumarono* (R), and *kumkumalāra* (V). *vāṭirī* (ABCD); cf. *vajravāṭirīye* (J), *vātiriye* and *lāvatīki* (R), and *vāṭīrī* (V). *kākajaṃghakī* (ABC); *kākajaṃghikī* (D); cf. *vajrakākajaṃghakīye* (J), *kākajaṃghakīye* and *kākajaṃghaki* (R), and *kākajaṅghakī* (V).

*sāmā* (A, B); *lāmā* (C); *samā* (D); cf. *vajrasamīye* (J), *sāmāraye* and *sāmā* (R), and *sāmā lehapiṣṭā ye hayistaye lohapṛṣṭā daddarī daddurī daddara sṛgālinī*. The color of the Yoginīs is like that of the *bhūcakra*; they should be known to have arms as before, consisting entirely of wisdom (*prajñā*). The supreme *Vāsinī* is the ground (*bhūmi*) that is very difficult to conquer (*sudurjayā*). The wheel of the lioness (*dvipini*) is considered to be threefold in nature; the third is of the nature of moisture-born beings (*saṃsveda*), and the fourth is the womb-born (*jarāyuja*), considered to be threefold in nature. I shall describe the second [wheel], that of the wind, from the outside: it is yellow in color by its own nature, adorned with thirty-six spokes. //134//
Now, the thirty-six Yoginīs who move upon the earth, in their proper order, are:
Siṃhī, Vyāghrī, Bhīmbhā, Śaśī, Gajī, Mṛgī, and Mārjārikī. //135//

The cow, the buffalo, the mare, the female jackal, the female rhinoceros, the yak, the female rat, the female donkey, the female sheep, the female goat, and the ewe are, respectively, [the mothers of the following]. //136//
Śvānī, Sūkarī, Bhallī, Daṇḍārī, Mūñjakī, Vesarā, Vilāṣī, Araṇyī, and Bṛhaśvānikā. //137//

Droṇakāki, Śārdūlī, Vyāḍā, Citriṇī, and Kuṭikā; by their natural colors and variegated markings, these belong to the Yoginīs who roam the earth. [The following are the animal forms: Lioness (Siṃhī), Tiger (Vyāghrī), Hyena (Bhīmbhā), Hare (Śaśī), Elephant (Gajī), Deer (Mṛgī), Cat (Mārjārikī), Cow (Gāvī), Buffalo (Mahiṣī), Mare (Turagī), Jackal (Jambukī), Gaṇḍī, Yak (Camara), Mouse (Mūṣī), Ass (Gardabhī), Sheep (Bheḍī), Goat (Ajakī), Ewe (Eḍakī); in sequence: Dog (Śvānī), Sow (Sūkarī), Bhallī, Daṇḍārī, Mūñjakī, Mule (Vesarā), Vilāṣī, Araṇyī, Bṛhaśvānikā, Droṇakāki, Śārdūlī, Vyāḍā, Vyāḍā, Citriṇī, Nakulī, Kṛkī, and Guhā. The latter is a dweller of villages. (138)
In this way, according to the colors [of the wheels], or again according to their respective colors, the goddesses whose nature is wisdom and means reside in the Upacchandoha. 139.
The stage is indeed Abhimukhī, and that is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); the inhabitants are those of the five continents, and the weapons and so forth are as before. //140//
The body is considered to have a natural female form and face;
it should be known [to be situated] at the eastern, northern, western, and southern gates. //141//
Brahmāṇī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Indrī, Caṇḍī, and Mahālakṣmī are located in those corners. //142//
The ḍākinīs and others are proclaimed by their forms and signs at the gates.

In the corners, the three lines should also be understood as being like [the goddesses] Dāḍhī and the others; for here [they are]: *Vajracitrinīye*, *citranīye* (J), *citriṇī* (R), and *citrāṇī* (V); *Nakulī* (ABCD); cf. *vajranakulīye* (J), *nakuliye* (R), and *nakulī* (V); *Kṛkī* (ABCD); cf. *vajrakṛkāyai* (J), *kṛkīye* (R), and *kṛkī* (V); *Guhā* (AB); *grahā* (C); *guhī* (D); cf. *vajraguhīye* (J), *guhāya* (R), and *guhā* (V); *Grāmanivāsinī* (ABCD); cf. *vajragrāmavasinīye* (J), *grāmanivāsinīye* (R), and *grāmavāsinī* (V); *Parā* (AB); *parām* (C); *ṣarā* (D).

[The one] dwelling in the fifth continent—A; *pañcadvīpa* BD; *pamcadvīpa* C; *kroñcadvīpaḥ* is noted in the upper margin of the leaf in A. ◊ *-nivāsī* ] ACD; *nipāsī* B. *Āyudhādi* ] ABD; *āyuvādi* C. *śarīra* ] ABCD; cf. *śarīra* R and V. ◊ *stryā-* ] A; *tryā* BCD. ◊ *-rūpa* ] ABD; *rūpam* C; cf. *rūpaṃ* R and *rūpa* V. ◊ *vaktram* ] ApcBCD; *ka* Aac. *svābhāvikam* ] AC; *svāsvā* Bac; *svāvāvika* Bpc; *svābhāmikam* D. ◊ *-paścimo ca* ] ABD; *paścime ca* C. ◊ *-dvāreṣu* ] ABCD.

Vārāhī, Indrī, Caṇḍī, and Mahālakṣmī [are to be placed] in the corners; [the syllable] *tat* [is to be placed] there. *Divajra*.

The [signs of] form (rūpa) are proclaimed in the corners (koṇakeṣu). That ground facing [the center] is indeed the Perfection of Wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). It possesses firmness and so forth, like a line (rekha-vat). Herein—A, B, C; atrata D.

The beautiful wheel of Dharma resides within the phenomena of body, speech, and mind; indeed, the cremation grounds are described as being in the center of the fire-wheels. One should place the fierce cremation ground—which causes death, terror, and fear of great terrors—within the counter-clockwise rotations. Furthermore, one should place the rites of expulsion, inciting hatred, muteness, and immobilization [in the other wheels].

One should cause trees to be planted in the corners starting from Īśāna in due order: first the *pūga*, the *akṣoṭaka*, the *nālīra*, the *dāḍima*, and the *bilvaka*; then the *āmalaka* and the *bījora*, O Rudra—one should arrange them according to this sequence. One should cause the guardians of the world (*lokapālinī*) to be assigned: Indrāṇī, Yamā, Rudrā, Yakṣiṇī, Bhūtinī, Ṛṣī, Rākṣasī, and Vāyubhāryā. One should by all means cause Nāginī and Meghinī to be assigned there for all [the directions].

589–607. The third wheel of knowledge (*jñānacakra*) is the caste (*varṇa*) of the Asuras, according to the lineage succession (*kulakrama*). [The Yoginīs are: Tilottamā, Atisukhā, Āpsarasā (ending in *ā* or used as such), Mahārātā, Ratirātākhyā, Padminī, Śaṅkhinī, Citriṇī, Gajā, Mahārūpā, Surūpā, Kāntivilāsinī, Sukhā, Puṣpakāmī, Kumudī, Nīlotpalā, Sundarī, Rāgā, Mahārāgā, Mahārāmakā, Madanā, Madanapriyā, Kāminī, Mahākāmikā, Sukhodbhavā, Sukhamatī, Priyatamā, Premakā, Saubhagyamatī, Saubhāgyā, Meṇukā, and Pradyumukhī. (181–182) They are declared to be of various castes and forms, the supreme leaders among Yoginīs. All of them consist of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*), and their castes are likewise of many kinds. (182) Their arms and weapons are to be known as before; the ground is Sādhumatī. The cremation grounds (*śmaśāna*) are radiant with jewels, producing the bliss of the Self-Arisen (*svayambhū*). (183) Therefore, the Sambhogakāya is the mandala consisting of three wheels (*tricakra*). It has four lines all around, due to the purification of the four joys (*caturānanda*). (184) In the four gates starting from the east, one should place the Yoginīs in sequence: Gaurī, Caurī, Vetālī, and Ghasmarī. (185) Furthermore, the four goddesses dwelling in the corners—Pukkasī, Śabarī, Caṇḍālī, and Ḍombinī—are always to be understood in the same order as before. (186) [The names are repeated: Sukhodbhavā, Sukhamatī, Priyatamā, Premakā, Saubhagyamatī, Saubhāgyā, Meṇukā, and Pradyumukhī. (187) [The names are repeated: Jātirūpī, -ātmakā, varṇa, -yudham (as before), bhūmi, Sādhumatī, śmaśānam, svayambhū-, -sukha-, -rekhā, samantā ca, -rānanda-, -śuddhitaḥ. (188) [The names are repeated: The four Yoginīs: Gaurī, Caurī, Vetālī, Ghasmarī. The four [corners]: Pukkasī, Śabarī, Caṇḍālī, Ḍombinī. (189) Outside, in the middle of the Knowledge Mandala (*jñānamaṇḍala*), is the Wheel of Cremation Grounds (*śmaśānacakra*). It is surrounded by the death of children, devouring, terrible battle, and the sound of *hā hā*. (190) The Great Compassionate One should contemplate these in counter-clockwise order starting from the east: Dhūma, Andhakāra, Agni, Hāhārava, and Mahārava. (191)
609. *Vṛkṣa* refers to sandalwood, camphor, nutmeg, and cardamom. 610. *Nāgesara*, *campaka*, *kundara*, and *devadāruka*. (189)
One should perform one hundred thousand recitations for the guardians of the directions (Dikpālas), as well as for the Sun, the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn. //190//

613. One should know that the heads of the Daityas should be made with fierce faces; likewise, [the weapons] such as the flaming sword, the churikā dagger, the spear, the hoof-shaped blade, and the stone. 191.

Externally, one should contemplate the cemetery, the knowledge of the death of the fool, the devouring of the veil, the terrible battle, the terrible weapon, and the sound of "sva-dam-sva. As before, [one should contemplate] smoke, darkness, fire, the great cries of "hā-hā," the two Maras, the nutmeg (*jātīphala*), the *nāgakeśara*, the *campaka*, the *kundara* trees, the sun and Mars, the son of the moon (Mercury), Saturn and Jupiter, as well as the mouth, the fierce ones, the knife, and the hoof.
One should cause lightning to strike amidst the various weapons in the middle of the cremation ground (616).
A wise man should employ the sword, collyrium, pills, foot-ointment, elixirs, sandals, and the attainment of the subterranean realm (pātāla) (192–618).
Thus ends the third, the Jñānacakra.
The third enclosure is the Sambhoga-maṇḍala, consisting of three wheels.

Oṃ sumbha niṣumbha kāyikāṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa vācikāṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! One should emanate them from the nature of the cause. Having brought them forth with animal faces, one should summon them with wrathful forms and cover them from the city. Sumbha is commanded by the Vajrī: "Sumbha niṣumbha! Seize, seize! Make them seize, make them seize the mental afflictions! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!"

*Oṃ ānaya hoḥ bhagavān vajrajñānika hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!* One should establish [the deities] in the directions starting from the east within the midst of the vajra-fence (*vajrapañjara*). Below there should be the vajra-ground, and above, a lattice of arrows. Furthermore, within the *dharmodayā*, one should visualize the vajra-wall and the canopy (*vitāna*). That [fence] should be visualized as three, four, five, or six-cornered. One should place all of this in sequence within the four enclosures (*catuṣpuṭa*) respectively. *Oṃ gha gha ghātaya ghātaya sarvaduṣṭān phaṭ! Kīlaya kīlaya sarvapāpān phaṭ! Hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ! O Vajrakīla, Vajradhara commands: nail down the vajra-body, speech, and mind of all obstructors! Hūṃ phaṭ!* This is the mantra for nailing down (*kīlana*). *Oṃ vajramudgara vajrakīlākoṭaya hūṃ phaṭ!* This is the mantra for striking (*ākoṭana*). In this way, in all the wheels (*cakra*), the heroic Blessed Ones born of the families, the entire emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), and the yoginīs who are vessels of awakening—thus the body-wheel (*kāyacakra*), which is the nature of the three bodies (*trikāya*), together with the emanation, is the third. The fourth enclosure: *Gṛhṇāpaya gṛhṇāpaya [caitasikān]* (seize, seize the mental factors). Now he speaks of the sacred seats (*pīṭha*), secondary seats (*upapīṭha*), and so forth, in their proper order: The sacred seat is Pūrṇagiri, Jālandhara, Oḍḍiyāna, and Arbuda; likewise, Godāvarī is a secondary seat. Rāmeśvara, Devīkoṭa, and Mālava are secondary seats. Kāmarūpa, Oḍra, Triśakuna, and Kauśala are fields (*kṣetra*). Kaliṅga is a subsidiary field (*upakṣetra*), as are Lampāka, Kāñcī, and Himālaya. The Tathāgatas, the Tathāgatas! Oṃ hūṃ vajra oṃ hūṃ! O Yoginīs! Heruka! Bindu, subtle bindu, vajra-bindu, bindus, the twelve-wheel bindus, the thousand [petals] as a single bindu, the wheel, the nectar, the bodhicitta! Oṃ! Homage to the Blessed One, the Lord of Heroes, who resembles the great kalpa-ending fire; whose crown of matted hair is fierce; whose face is terrifying with fangs like a gaping maw; who is radiant with a thousand arms; who wields an axe, a noose, a raised trident, and a khaṭvāṅga; who wears a garment of tiger skin; whose body is a great mass of smoky darkness. Kara kara! Kuru kuru! Bandha bandha! Trāsaya trāsaya! Kṣobhaya kṣobhaya! Hraum hraum! Hraḥ hraḥ! Phem phem! Phaṭ phaṭ! Daha daha! Paca paca! Bhakṣa bhakṣa! To you who hang with garlands of fat, blood, and entrails—gṛhṇa gṛhṇa! The serpents and snakes dwelling in the seven underworlds—vā tarjaya tarjaya! Ākaḍḍha ākaḍḍha! Hrīm hrīm! Jñaum jñaum! Kṣmām kṣmām! Hām hām! Him him! Hum hum! Kili kili! Sili sili! Hili hili! Dhili dhili! Hum hum phaṭ! Gaurī, who is praised by all the Buddhas, is free from all duality, having abandoned all dualities. Gaurī, Caurī, Vetālī, Ghasmarī, Pukkasī, Śabarī, Caṇḍālī, and Ṭombī—meditate upon the Great Bliss mandala! Be intent on the stainless nature of all things, both internal and external. Know that very mandala to be bliss! With a great form of various aspects, emanate the mandala-cakra throughout the three worlds!
Then, from this, the great secret shall be explained.

"O Sovereign Sun, if you invite the world as your guest every day, for what reason have you entered into emptiness?
Arise! Arise! For I am of the nature of compassion!"
O Vajradhara, Great Bliss, please fulfill my desire! //25//
Listen, listen! The needs of others have vanished;
the world will become like cattle that have died.
Desire my blossoming lotus!
In this way, make the entire world become happy. //26//
O Vajradhara, sport with me!
May I attain the inexpressible innate nature.
Other beings in the world have become deluded.
Otherwise, how could your emptiness be rendered meaningless? //27//
You are the agent of all phenomena;
why do you abide in a state where the innate nature is beyond movement?
Grant me the desire for the supreme goal!
In this way, you act in harmony with the worlds. //28//

Thus, from the Great King of Tantras of the Glorious Ḍākinī Ocean Yoginī, this is the fifteenth chapter, which teaches the establishment of the Blessed One’s authentic meditative absorption and various instructions.
Thus it was said.
In the language of India: *Śrī-ḍākārṇava-tantra-maṇḍala-cakra-sādhanaratna-padmarāga-nidhi-nāma*.

In the language of Tibet: *Dpal mkha’ ’gro rgya mtsho’i rgyud kyi dkyil ’khor gyi ’khor lo’i sgrub thabs rin po che padma rā ga’i gter* (The Jewel Sādhana of the Maṇḍala Circle of the Glorious Ocean of Ḍākinīs Tantra, Entitled “The Treasure of the Padmarāga”).
Homage to the glorious Blessed One, Ḍākinī Ocean!
To you who are the embodiment of the essence that gathers the compassion of all Buddhas.
The nature that condenses all things into one, the innate face of the lineage-holder.
Non-dual wisdom, Vajravārāhī, and...
I bow to that one who dwells together [with me];
by the light rays of his words of wisdom, [he illuminates].
Dispelling the darkness of the minds of those who are worthy vessels.
I bow to the assembly of gurus,
such as Saroruha and others, who satisfy [beings] with the nectar of the ultimate meaning and who are like the moon.
The Stages of Visualization based on the Oral Instructions of the Glorious Ocean of Ḍākinīs (1v1),
and the Colophon of the *Ratnopāya* (35r7).
Although one lacks the capacity to realize it as it truly is,
I shall write this for my own recollection.

First, a practitioner who has been purified through the stages of the empowerment of the glorious *Ḍākinīsamudra* and who possesses deep conviction in the profound and vast [teachings], having realized the meaning of the tantra, should prepare a place for meditative concentration (*dhyānasthāna*) in a location devoid of people—such as a mountain, a mountain cave, a ravine, the shore of a great ocean, a primordially established charnel ground, or any other place that gladdens the mind. This site should be provided with the requisites of the Blessed One’s cloth painting (*paṭa*), ritual cakes (*bali*), the water for offerings (*arghya*), and so forth; it should be made delightful by sprinkling it with nectar (*amṛta*) and scattering flowers across the ground. At dawn, imagining that one is being exhorted by the songs and the sound of the hand-drum (*ḍamaru*) of the Vajrayoginīs, the practitioner performs the purification of the face and other rites. On the ground, either upon a corpse or on human skin upon which a crossed vajra (*viśvavajra*) has been drawn, the practitioner sits naked in the vajra posture (*vajraparyaṅka*) facing south, with a vessel of nectar placed before him. Grasping the fingers from the base of the middle finger to the little finger of the left hand with the armor-mantras of the heroines (*vīravatī*), he should place the armor-mantra of the Blessed One on the middle finger and the tips of the remaining fingers.

Then, fill a lotus vessel with *madana* (intoxicant) and place it in the palm of the right hand. With the left hand, draw the lines of a *dharmodaya* (source of phenomena), and by reciting the three syllables, visualize it as nectar. Joining the thumb and ring finger of that same hand, sprinkle the liquor; likewise, perform the purification bath for the five limbs, the sprinkling and drinking, and the cleansing offering (*bsang gtor*) for the ritual substances.

Then, in a vessel upon one's face, one should smear a square maṇḍala with that very liquor mixed with fragrant substances in front of oneself; having scattered loose flowers and touched it with the vajra-mudrā while reciting *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, one consecrates it as the nature of the subterranean realm, the earth, and the heavens.
Then, reciting "oṃ āḥ sthānaṃ me rakṣa hūṃ," one should protect the site by placing a single flower beneath oneself.
Reciting "Oṃ āḥ protect my self hūṃ," one should place a single flower upon one's head and thus protect oneself.
One should protect oneself through the embrace mudrā and by reciting: *oṃ āḥ yogam me rakṣa hūṃ*.

1199 *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*. [Emendation]; *bhur bhu wa swaḥ* D; *bhur bhu ba swaḥ* P. *sthānam* [Emendation]; *sthā năm* DP (*rang gi* D; *rang gis* P). *om* P; *a* D. *ātmānam* [Emendation]; *ātmā nām* DP. *yogam* P; *yo gām* D. 198 Following that, one generates the thought: "In order to establish sentient beings who are submerged in the ocean of suffering of saṃsāra upon the level of Mahāmudrā, I shall meditate on the glorious Ḍākārṇava. Thus one arouses the mind of awakening.
Then, while reciting the mantras of the hero’s armor over the ordinary body itself, one should don the armor by touching those respective locations with the vajra-mudrā.
Then, with palms joined holding flowers, [one should] turn:
"The glorious Vajraḍākinī,
by means of the wheel of ḍākinīs, possesses the five wisdoms and the three bodies."
Homage to the Protector of Beings!
As many as there are Vajra Ḍākinīs,
who sever the bonds of conceptual thought and engage thoroughly in worldly activities.
I constantly prostrate to all those [beings] as numerous as that.
Completely submerged in the ocean of existence.
By whatever grace of the sublime guru, who is skilled in perfectly delivering [beings],...
I desire to generate this primordial wisdom within myself.
By saying "I... [D; my... P], one should clearly bring to mind the *ḍākas*, *ḍākinīs*, and spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) with the mind, scatter flowers, and prostrate.
Then, one should offer the torma as explained in the ritual manual.

In the same way, the meditation upon oneself as Cakrasaṃvara—four-faced and twelve-armed, blue in color, together with Vārāhī—in an instant before the Blessed One and his retinue, is the purification of the body.

From the complete transformation of the syllable *pam* at one’s own heart, there arises a multicolored eight-petaled lotus; upon that, from the complete transformation of the syllable *ram*, there arises a sun mandala.

Visualize a wheel and upon it the syllable *hūṃ*, black in color and the nature of the five wisdoms, radiating multicolored rays of light. Reciting the *āli* and *kāli* vowels and consonants, preceded by *oṃ* at the beginning and followed by *hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ* at the end, one draws forth from the *nāda* of the *hūṃ* a garland of multicolored syllables. These encircle the upper part of the left side of the body with a blue garland, the middle with a red garland, and the lower part with a white garland. From these, the hosts of deities belonging to the three realms are emanated in successive order—upper, middle, and lower—and scattered. From them, the classes of the formless, form, and desire realms are projected; having cleared away the obstructors of the three realms, their reabsorption into their respective abodes constitutes the purification of speech.

Then, one should visualize the four syllables of Śrī Heruka—blue in color—in the space above the crown of the head, the forehead, the throat, and the region of the heart, and recollect their meaning as follows:
"The syllable ŚRĪ is the meaning of all that arises; it is asserted as the nature of both the outer and the inner."
All these are conventional forms,
as well as that which consists of the culmination of bliss without entering.
Even non-duality, such as E-Vaṃ and so forth, is likewise.
The definitive expression of the syllable *śrī* is *e vam*. From the heart, the syllable *he* completely [emanates] Heruka and his own retinue.
From the source of all meditations, grasping and the rest are produced;
that is the nature of the empty cause, the non-conceptual nature of the cause.
The nature of phenomena is selflessness;
that is the abiding of the yoga of emptiness.
The arrangement is the selflessness of persons.
The great net of conceptual construction—
The syllable *ru*, which is of the nature of a condition,
is my own state free from conceptual elaboration (*prapañca*). Furthermore, it expresses all letters without exception.
I know that which is beyond duality.
Because it does not abide in anything whatsoever,
it is therefore expressed as *ka*.
Thus it is said: "The entity is not empty of direct perception;
its nature is that of mere entity.
O Goddess, you who abide as the glorious Heruka!"
That which has been previously cultivated is universal.
To recite these words and bring their meaning to mind is what purifies the mind.
Then, one should meditate on the divine pride of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
Then, the aggregate of form is Vairocana.
The aggregate of feeling is Vajrasūrya.
The aggregate of perception is Padmanarteśvara.
The aggregate of formations is Vajrarāja.
The aggregate of consciousness is Vajrasattva.
The very essence of all Tathāgatas is Śrī Heruka Vajra.
The eyes are the vajra of delusion (*moha*).
The listeners are Hatred Vajra.
The nose is the Vajra of Envy.
Khaḍga is Rāgavajra.
The regent was Ser sna Rdo rje.
All sense bases are Īśvaravajra.
The earth element is that which causes falling.
The water element is murderous.
My element is the summoner.
The wind element is Lāsyā.
The element of space is Padmārciṣmatī.
These should also be understood according to the arrangement set forth by the master Prajñāpālita.

Then, preceded by the clapping of the left index finger and thumb: *oṃ sumbha niḥsumbha kāyikāṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ* / *oṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa vācikāṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ* / *oṃ gṛhṇāpaya gṛhṇāpaya caitasikāṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ* /
Oṃ ānaya hoḥ! O Blessed One, possessor of vajra-gnosis, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!

*Gsod ma* (D); *bsod ma* (P). Then (D); *da nas* (P). The index finger (D); *'dzub mo* (P). *Sumbha nisumbha* (corr.); *sum bha ni sum bha* (DP). *Kāyikām* (em.); *kā yi kam* (DP); cf. *kāyikām* in the *Dākārṇava*. First *hūṃ* (D); *hum* (P). First *gr̥hṇa* (D); *gr hna* (P). First *hūṃ* (D); *hum* (P). *Caitasikām* (em.); *tsi tā kam tsa ra si mam* (D); *tsa ra si mam* (P); cf. *caitasikāṃ* in the *Ṣaḍaṅgayoga-ṭīkā*. First *hūṃ* (D); *hum* (P). *Bhagavān* (D); *bha ga wan* (P). *Jñānikāṃ* (em.); *dznyā ni kam* (DP); cf. *jñānikāṃ* in the *Ṣaḍaṅgayoga-ṭīkā*. First *hūṃ* (D); *hum* (P). By reciting these [mantras], from the *hūṃ* at the heart, there emanate [rays] having black, green, red, and yellow colors. From the limit of Brahmā down to the golden foundation of the earth, one should visualize the great forms of the mantras emanating sequentially, facing outward toward the eastern, northern, western, and southern directions.

Then, from the complete transformation of the syllable *raṃ* below oneself, one should visualize a sun mandala. Upon this, from the complete transformation of a blue *hūṃ*, there arises a very great crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*) reaching down to the golden ground, consecrated by the *hūṃ*. Through its light rays and the light rays of mantras such as *sumbhala*, one should visualize a square enclosure (*prākāra*) of vajra-nature with colors corresponding to those mentioned before; above the vajras and the light rays of the *hūṃ*, a lattice-work of green five-pointed vajra-arrows; and beneath that, a vajra pavilion and canopy.

[The ground] P; [the fourth ground] D. *Sumbha* P; *Sum-bha* D. Then, from the four mantras beginning with *Sumbha*, there arise the four goddesses such as Khavakāsyā (Vulture-Faced One) and so forth; and from *Oṃ*, *Hūṃ*, *Hūṃ*, and *Phaṭ*, there arise the four goddesses such as Yamamathani (Slayer of Yama) and so forth. These have one face and two arms; with their right hands they hold vajra-hammers, and with their left hands they hold, from the navel downward, kīlas in the form of goddesses identical to themselves. They hold curved knives (*kartṛ*) in their right hands and skull-cups (*kapāla*) in their left hands. To them [one recites]: *sarvavighnān ānaya jaḥ*.

By reciting these words, the hosts of obstructing spirits who have gone to the cardinal and intermediate directions are summoned outside the enclosure. Within it, one should visualize eight *hūṃ*s corresponding to the colors of the directional guardians. The hosts of obstructing spirits are absorbed into the *hūṃ*s, and from their transformation, the eight directional guardians are generated.

Then, by proclaiming a forceful and long-drawn *hūṃ*, one visualizes a great fire pit before each of them. The goddesses cast them into those pits and strike them from the head with ritual daggers (*kīla*), reciting: *oṃ gha gha ghātaya ghātaya sarvaduṣṭān phaṭ | kīlaya kīlaya sarvapāpān phaṭ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ vajrakīla vajradharo ājñāpayati vighnānāṃ kāyavākcittavajraṃ kīlaya hūṃ phaṭ*.
By reciting these words three times, one should also strike the throat and the heart.

Then, by reciting "Oṃ vajramudgara vajra vajrakīlākoṭaya hūṃ phaṭ" three times, one should imagine that they are struck with a vajra hammer; having been deprived of the life-force associated with conceptual thought, they attain non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*). One should then visualize the goddesses dissolving into the enclosure, and subsequently, the circular enclosures of fire, vajra, lotus, and wheel as a single, unified whole in successive order from the outside.
From the melting of the *hūṃ* above, one should cultivate the pride: "The space is filled without interval by minute vajras, and thus I and all wandering beings are entirely free from obstacles."

Then, light rays emanating from the seed syllable at the heart invite the Guru and the mandala of Śrī Ḍākinīsaṃudra; they should be visualized as seated in the center of the previously prepared maṇḍala.
Then, one should perform the purification by reciting "oṃ āḥ hūṃ" three times.
With the mantra "Oṃ pravarasatkārapādyaṃ pratīccha svāhā," one should offer water for washing the feet at the [deity's] feet.

With the mantra "oṃ pravarasatkārārghaṃ pratīccha svāhā," one should offer the water for the feet (*pādya*) three times at [the deity's] feet, using the mudrā of opening from the left hand, with the thumb and ring finger forming the shape of a conch shell holding flowers.
In that manner, one should offer flowers into the maṇḍala with their respective mantras.

Oṃ āḥ hūṃ svāhā svāhā! Accept this respectful offering of water (argha); accept it for all of us! Oṃ āḥ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ; oṃ āḥ vajradhūpe hūṃ; oṃ āḥ vajradīpe hūṃ; oṃ āḥ vajragandhe hūṃ; oṃ āḥ vajranaivedye hūṃ—with these [mantras], one should also perform the offerings.

I shall rejoice in the merit accumulated by the śrāvakas, the solitary lions, the unsurpassed Victors, and the Sons of the Victors, and I shall perfectly dedicate it toward awakening.

From the complete transformation of the syllable *yam* in the lower portion within that [mandala], there arises a blue wind mandala shaped like a bow, with two banners (*dhvaja*) fluttering at its two ends; it is consecrated by the syllable *yam*.

Inside that [enclosure], at the bottom, the syllable *yam* appears in dark blue; it transforms into a wind-wheel, which is dark blue, bow-shaped, equipped with fluttering banners at both ends, and marked with *yam*.
Above that, from the complete transformation of a red letter RAM, there arises a red triangular fire mandala with blazing edges, consecrated by the syllable RAM.
Above that, from the complete transformation of a white BAṂ, there arises a white, circular water mandala together with a vase, marked with the syllable BAṂ.
Above that, from the complete transformation of a yellow path, there arises a yellow square earth mandala, marked with three-pointed vajras at its corners and consecrated by the syllable *laṃ*.

Upon that, from the complete transformation of the three syllables of various colors, there arises Mount Meru, four-sided and possessing eight peaks, composed of the nature of the four precious substances and blessed by the three syllables.

Above that, from the complete transformation of the syllable BAṂ, there is a multicolored lotus; upon that, from the complete transformation of the syllable HŪṂ, one visualizes a crossed vajra (*viśvavajra*). The elements melt and become of a nature that is supple, and by merging into one, they fall beneath Mount Meru.
From the complete transformation of the mass of melted elements resting upon the crossed vajra, there arises the celestial mansion (*vimāna*) endowed with four tiers of gates.

The exterior of all is the purity of the five wisdoms; externally, it is accompanied by white.

Oṃ na haṃ nā hāṃ ni hiṃ nī hīṃ nu huṃ nū hūṃ ne heṃ nai haiṃ no hoṃ nau hauṃ naṃ haṃ naḥ haḥ | oṃ ha vaṃ hā vāṃ hi viṃ hī vīṃ hu vuṃ hū vūṃ he veṃ hai vaim ho voṃ hau vaum | [In counter-clockwise direction: na haṃ no hoṃ nau hauṃ | Gshin-rje-ma’s: hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ | phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ | svāhā svāhā.

Upon the sun at the crown of the head: *oṃ sva hram svā hrām svi hrim svi hrīm svu hrum svūm hrūm sve hrem svai hraim svo hrom svau hraum svam hram svaḥ hraḥ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā svāhā*.
This is red and white in color, the essence of Padmanarteśvara and Mohanī.

*svā hrām svi hrim svi hrīm svu hrum svūm hrūm sve hrem svai hraim svo hrom svau hraum svam hram svaḥ hraḥ hūm hūm hūm hūm. phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ, svāhā svāhā.* Within the two upper arms, upon the sun: *om va hram vā hrām vi hrim vī hrīm vu hrum vū hrūm ve hrem vai hraim vo hrom vau hraum vam hram vaḥ hraḥ hūm hūm hūm hūm phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā svāhā.*
This means that the blackish-yellow [deities] are Heruka and Kṣobhaṇī.
Oṃ va hram vā hrām vi hrim vī hrīm vu hrum vū hrūm ve hrem vai hraim vo hrom vau hraum vam hram vaḥ hraḥ hūm hūm hūm hūm phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā svāhā.
Upon the sun disk of the second eye: oṃ hūm hūm ham ham hām hām him him hīm hīm hum hum hūm hūm hem hem haim haim hom hom haum haum ham ham hah haḥ hūm hūm hūm hūm phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā svāhā.
Those called [such] are reddish-green Vajrasūryā and Trāsanī.

Within the area of the ūrṇā-kośa (the hair-treasure between the brows), upon the sun, [is] *oṃ phaṭ phaṭ pha pha phā phā phi phi phī phī phu phu phū phū phe phe phai phai pho pho phau phau pham pham phah phah hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā svāhā*.

These are greenish-smoky in color, like a supreme horse and a fierce woman. From these, a collection of syllables radiates out, such that from the soles of the feet up to the crown of the head, they become its subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*).

Oṃ phaṭ phaṭ pha pha pha pha phi phi phi phi phu phu phu phu phe phe phai phai pho pho phau phau pham pham phaḥ phaḥ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ, phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ, svāhā svāhā; outside the body, there is a white Oṃ Ha at the heart and a yellow Nama Hi at the head.
Svāhā hu, red, at the crown of the head;
Vauṣaṭ he, black, on the two shoulders; Hūṃ hūṃ ho, orange-red, on the two eyes.
Phat ham! It is greenish-blue in all its limbs.
HŪM HŪM HO HŪM HŪM THAD KA’I OM PHAT PHAT DUD KHA BAR DU PHAṬ HAM / PHAṬ PHAṬ DPUNG PA LJANG GU RDO RJE PHAG MO’I LTE BAR OM VAM DMAR PO DANG / HĀM YOM SNGON MO SNYING GAR RO //
Hrīṃ mom! O white one, to your mouth!
Hrem Hrīm is for the yellow [deity].
Hum hūm, green, at the crown of the head.
Phaṭ phaṭ! Visualize the syllable DU at the junction of the eyebrows; from it, light rays radiate forth, filling the entire body.
Then, from that crown of the head, one should become non-dual with the maṇḍala of primordial wisdom;
furthermore, this is done by circling the blazing mudrā at the forehead.
Pressing the right leg with the left,
one invites the great mandala accomplished by the light rays of the seed-syllable at the heart into the space before oneself,
and performs perfect offerings with the lute goddesses and others emanated from the seed-syllable.
By "jaḥ," they are summoned above their respective [seats];
by "hūṃ," they are made to enter, like water merging into water.
One should pacify with *vaṃ* and gladden with *hoḥ*.

HĀM HRĪṂ HRĪṂ VAṂ. Then, once again, light rays from the seed syllable at one's own heart invite immeasurable deities of the five families appearing in the attire described in the *Śrī Guhyasamāja*. Having made offerings to them with the lute goddess (*vīṇā*) and others, [one recites]: "Just as the Tathāgatas were bathed immediately upon their birth,"
In the same way, may I be bathed;
purify me with the water of the gods.
When this supplication was made,
all the Buddhas of the ten directions were drawn into their mouths by the sound of the bliss of those [deities] entering meditative equipoise; having melted,
they emerged through the vajra path.
One should sprinkle everyone with the stream of self-arisen nectar that emerges from between the lotus of the goddess and [one's own].
Then, with water and so forth, I shall bathe Tathāhaṃ with pure, divine water. Then, from the drops of water on the crowns of all the gods, the visualization of the Lord is as follows:
Akṣobhya is the principal [deity].
On Vārāhī is Amitābha.
To the Lotus Ḍākinīs, Ratnasambhava.
For the goddesses of the gates and intermediate directions, it is Amoghasiddhi.
For those belonging to the Vajracakra family, it is Akṣobhya.
For those belonging to the heart-wheel, Amitābha.
To those who possess the wheel of qualities, he appears as Vairocana.
For those belonging to the space wheel, there is Akṣobhya.
For those who revolve upon the wheel of wind, there is the sound of drums.
For those belonging to the earth wheel, it is Ratnasambhava.
For those belonging to my mandala, Amitābha.
To those who revolve in the wheel of water, [I am] the Buddha.
To those belonging to the wheel of primordial wisdom, there is the sound of the drum.
For those belonging to the wheel of the mind, it is Akṣobhya.
For those belonging to the wheel of speech, Amitābha.
For those belonging to the wheel of the Body, it is that of the Buddha; they assume the form of the Nirmāṇakāya.
It does not exist for anyone throughout all the Fortunate Aeon.
Then the five families, having uttered "Oṃ sarvatathāgatābhiṣekasamayaśriye hūṃ," dissolved into the lords.
Then, having emanated countless goddesses such as Mālavī and Gaurī, who have issued forth from one's own seed-syllables,
one should offer worship to all the mandalas.
Furthermore:
"Gaurī holds a deer and a bow."
Tsaurīmani is the vessel of the sun; Betālī is the hand of water.
The holder of medicine is Ghasmarī.
Pukkasi, the one with powerful arms.
Just as Śabarī holds her staff, Caṇḍālī likewise proclaims it at Madhura.
Embracing from the throat, she is Ḍombinī.
Thus it is said.
It is not clear; those [lines] should also be understood as follows: "With all characteristics complete..."
Great bliss and so forth, the excellent,
and the complete abandonment of duality.
The offering, which is the nature of the three realms,
is performed with all things that arise.
Then those goddesses will offer a mantra-praise. What are they? Oṃ śrīvajra-he-he-ru-ru-kam hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ ḍākinījālaśamvara svāhā.
This is the heart-mantra of the Blessed One.
Oṃ hrīḥ ha ha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. This is the near-heart mantra.
The goddesses of the Rūpa and Arūpa realms and so forth constitute the eight lines.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the Lord of Heroes, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, to him who resembles the fire at the end of a great aeon, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ, to him whose crown is a mass of matted locks, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, to the one with a mouth terrifyingly fierce with fangs, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ, to the one resplendent with a thousand arms, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, to the one wielding an axe, a noose, a raised trident, and a khaṭvāṅga staff, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, to the one wearing a tiger-skin garment, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, to the one whose body is like great smoky darkness, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, homage to the glorious Vajraḍāka, the Great Hero, the Lord of Heroes, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, to the one who causes even the trembling of the three worlds to tremble, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!

Oṃ, to the one with a hundred thousand eyes, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!

Oṃ koṭilakṣabhujāya hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, to him who clings to and is licked by a garland of flames, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, to him who raises a battle-axe, a noose, and a trident, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, to him whose fierce body is smoke-colored like the end of an eon, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, to the one with a gaping mouth who utters "hā hā," hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, to the mantra filled by the assembly of Mothers, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, to the one whose hand holds Sahajasundarī as his beloved, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ hūṃ hūṃkāroccāraṇamukhāya hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ mahāśmaśānapriyāya hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ sarvabhūtasamtrāsanakarāya hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, to the one with the splendor of the fire at the end of the great eon, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ, to the one with a crown of matted locks, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, to the bearer of the khaṭvāṅga, skull-cup, and trident, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, to the one girdled by the great ocean, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ, to the wearer of a tiger-skin garment, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, to the crusher of the hosts of vetālas, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, to the one who wards off great obstacles, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ, to the one who crushes enemies, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, to the one who dwells within the single hair-pore of the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, to the one with a hundred thousand faces, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, to the one with the radiance of the ocean of gnosis, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!

Oṃ, to the one whose roar shakes Mount Sumeru, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, to the bearer of the wrathful form, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, to the self whose essence is the tilaka of the great space, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, for the accomplishment of thousands of millions of Buddhas in a single instant, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, for the raining down of the nectar of primordial wisdom, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, for the setting in motion of all activities, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, for the one who binds, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ, for the one who shatters all conceptual constructions, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, to the one whose body is adorned with a garland of skulls, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, to the destroyer of mantras and yantras created by others, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, to the performer of great protection, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!

Oṃ, to the self of the Indra-jāla of all sentient beings, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, to the Great-Minded One who proclaims the discourse that devours [all] speech, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!

To the crown of matted hair, MASA MASA GASA GASA RASA RASA BHARA BHARA MAṬA MAṬA TRAṬA TRAṬA GHATA GHATA MUÑCA MUÑCA! O you who delight in terrible darkness, PHIM PHIM PHUDA PHUDA! Kill, kill! O you whose form is ultimate reality, to the performer of peace, to the increaser of prosperity, to the one in the form of a world-protector, to the one in the form of all bodies, to trees, shrubs, and creepers, to the one in all forms, to all things, to the form of death, to the form of consumption, to the form of devouring, to the incomparable one, to the incomparable face, JĀTI JĀTI! Subdue, subdue the gods! For the sake of all bodies, to Anala, to Vāyu, to the remover of all diseases, to Kālāgni, to Daitya, to the Eye, to the Protector, TRAṬA TRAṬA PHUDA PHUDA MARA MARA! O you whose form is ultimate reality, to the increaser of prosperity, to the one in the form of a world-protector, to the shrub, to the one in all forms, to the incomparable one, to the face, HASA HASA VILASA VILASA! Then, furthermore, the one called Kṣudraheruka becomes yellowish-red in color; the vajra-wheel becomes the heart-wheel, and one should meditate on it within the heart-wheel.
Then, furthermore, the one called Padmaheruka becomes reddish-white in color; the heart-wheel becomes the wheel of all qualities, and one should meditate on it within the wheel of all qualities.
Then again, that which is called the Heruka of Space becomes blue; having become the wheel of all qualities, the wheel of space, one should meditate on the wheel of space within.

Then again, at the end, that which is called the Heruka of Wind becomes blue with various colors; the wheel of space having passed into the wheel of wind, one should meditate on the wheel of wind within.
Then again, the Lord known as Earth-Heruka becomes yellow; the wind-mandala enters the earth-mandala, and one should meditate on the earth-mandala within.
Then again, the blazing Heruka becomes red; the earth-mandala becomes the fire-mandala, and one should meditate on the fire-mandala within.
Then again, that which is called Water Heruka becomes white; the fire wheel transforms into a water wheel, and one should meditate on it as being within all the water wheels.
Then again, that which is called Wisdom Heruka becomes multicolored; the water wheel transforms into a wisdom wheel, and one should meditate on the wisdom wheel as having come within.
Then, one should again meditate on the so-called Citta-Heruka as black; the wisdom-wheel (jñānacakra) becomes the mind-wheel (cittacakra), and one should meditate on the mind-wheel within.
Then, the so-called Vāk-Heruka becomes the color of vermilion; the [deities] of the mind-wheel become the speech-wheel (vākcakra), and one should meditate on the speech-wheel within.

Then again, the Heruka of the Body becomes a color blended of blue, red, and white; those belonging to the Wheel of Speech become the Wheel of the Body, and one should meditate on them within the Wheel of the Body.
By circling in this manner eleven times, one should continue until they have entered within the Vajra Wheel.
Thereafter, one should meditate upon oneself as the Ocean of Dakinis itself.
